Wang Meng 葛稚川移居圖 · animation notes

Depth on Silk

Depth Anything V2 fails on this painting's landscape and succeeds on its figures — and the reason it splits that way decides which parts of the animation a model can ever help with.

16 August 2026 · six measurements, each against a null

What was tested

  1. Monocular depth reads the landscaperefuted
  2. Monocular depth gives a figure volumeconfirmed
  3. Depth cuts the deer's legs for freerefuted
  4. The scroll-scale plane stack works inside one shotrefuted
  5. Grading a plane stack beats flat cardsrefuted
  6. A figure can walk further than the frame is wideconfirmed

Finding 01

The landscape is a vertical ramp

refuted

Depth Anything V2 can read this painting's space.

This was measured on 13 August and retired; the depth map itself had been left in /tmp and was gone, so it was regenerated. The failure is sharper than the original note claimed.

55% of the depth variance is explained by image row alone. The residual is almost entirely figures and foliage. The cliff, the gorge, the ledge, the river and the entire trestle bridge are absent — the bridge Ge Hong is standing on does not exist in the model's map.

The mechanism matters more than the verdict. A Yuan hanging scroll encodes space by overlap, contour and 留白, with stacked viewpoints and no station point. The model has no prior for a layout that was never photographed. What it does instead is object segmentation — which is the same verdict SAM returned on this painting a session earlier, arrived at independently.

Finding 02

The same model sculpts the man

confirmed

Depth can give a cut-out figure real volume.

Ryan's proposal: stop asking the model for the scene and ask it for the figures, so a walking puppet stops being a flat card. Tested on Ge Hong, cut from the master at native resolution.

Ge Hong · relief against a flat-card null
measurevaluenull
relief after removing a tilted plane0.06980.0000
relief ÷ standoff from background0.250.00
corr(depth, ink luminance)−0.064±1.0 = tracing ink
corr(depth, blurred luminance)−0.081±1.0 = tracing wash

The last two rows are the ones that make it believable. The obvious failure on an ink painting is a model reading black robe-borders as grooves and handing back a darkness map dressed as relief. At −0.06 it is not doing that. It is completing a shape from silhouette and fold lines with no shading to read.

Depth where there is a shape prior; convention where there is not. A standing robed human is a category the model has seen a million times. A Yuan gorge is a grammar it has never seen once.

An earlier run of this same test returned −0.38, which looked like contamination. That was a bad mask, not a bad model: mask/gehong holds four scraps — fan, sleeve, hem, hat — and the scraps are mostly black robe border. On the full figure the effect vanishes.

What it is worth

The volume is the smallest prize. The gait currently keys its hem-shear off how far down the figure a pixel sits, because that was the only depth proxy available; with a real map it keys off actual depth, so the near side of the robe swings further than the far shoulder. That is the difference between a paper doll bending and cloth moving. A figure with relief can also take a slight yaw as it walks, which a flat cutout cannot.

Finding 03

The deer keeps its legs

refuted

Depth will separate the pack-animal's legs, so they need not be cut by hand.

The deer is the blocked item: a quadruped's legs are visible, and the shear built for a robe hem thins and smears them. They want cutting as separate parts with their own pivots and phases. If depth separated them, that cut would come free.

The reason is in the painting, not the model: the far legs are barely painted, so there is nothing to resolve. Connected components on the leg band returned one blob.

The purple foreleg reads at depth 0.325 while the far flank reads 0.497. Higher is nearer, so the model has placed the near foreleg behind the far side of the body. Displacing the deer with this map would send its legs through its own belly.

That inversion is the classic monocular artifact — thin dark strokes on light silk get pushed back. The deer's legs stay a hand-cut job. Depth saves a little work (the antlers, one leg, a near/far body split) and cannot be trusted below the barrel.

Finding 04

The plane stack is the wrong size

refuted

The existing 17-plane VLM stack can supply landscape depth for a shot.

DepthFlow accepts an external map — scene.input(image=…, depth=…), normalised, near white — so it never had to estimate anything. The plan was to hand it the VLM-authored plane stack, where a language model read the pictorial convention a depth model cannot.

Over this shot that stack is two blobs: 69.6% of pixels are a single plane (figures-path) and 21.2% are the cliff behind it. It was authored for a Z-flight down the whole 6586×15923 scroll, so its planes are scroll-sized features and one 720×1280 shot sits inside one or two of them. It encodes depth between shots, not within one.

Re-planning at shot scale fixes it. Eleven planes on the first pass left 26.5% unclaimed, concentrated in the mid-ground band that matters — the deer got no plane at all, and nearest-fill then handed it the depth of the far river. A review pass brought it to thirteen planes.

Finding 05

A soft edge does not make a surface

refuted

Grading a plane stack escapes the flat-card look under a Z-push.

This was the whole argument for feeding an authored map to a ray-marching renderer: cards look flat under a push, a graded surface would not. Rendering both with a z-buffered forward splat, which leaves disocclusion holes visible rather than smearing over them:

Push-in, zoom 0.18 · holes uncovered at the final frame
depth mapholestrue disocclusion
constant depth (null — no parallax possible)24.8%—
flat cards, 3 levels25.0%0.2 pts
graded 13-plane map25.5%0.7 pts

Without the constant-depth null the 25% would have read as catastrophic tearing; almost all of it is splat lattice, not disocclusion. With the null, graded and cards are the same number — and both are under one point of real disocclusion, meaning the parallax is barely doing anything.

Corrected 16 Aug, after publishing. The first version of this null was itself wrong, and it inflated the result. Normalising a constant depth map divided by its own zero range, so the null came out all-black rather than mid-grey and therefore zoomed at a lower rate than the map it was controlling for — fewer splat gaps, 11.4%, and an apparent 14 points of disocclusion that did not exist. A null that is not matched on everything except the effect is not a null. The conclusion is unchanged and in fact stronger; the numbers above are the corrected ones.

Measuring why they match gives the mechanism. For every one of the thirteen planes, the interior deviates 0.0% from its nominal depth. A Gaussian grade only moves a band near the boundaries.

Blurring a plane stack does not create a surface. It feathers the seams. A card with a soft edge is still a card — which is why the graded map measured and looked identical to explicit flat cards.

This closes the loop on the original note. DepthFlow consumes a depth map and does not produce one; handing it an authored plane map hands it cards, because piecewise-constant depth is what a plane stack is. Tilting the planes was already tried and rejected — oriented planes read as skewing cutouts and worsen the mask seams. The Z-push into this painting stays unsolved, and now the reason is specific rather than atmospheric: every depth source available gives piecewise-constant landscape depth, and piecewise-constant depth is cards.

Finding 06

The walk is now as long as the painting

confirmed

A figure can walk further than the frame is wide.

The recorded limit was that travel past roughly 70px walks the figure out of a 720-wide frame. The answer is the cel one: the plate is a strip cut from the master at the shot's own scale, wider and taller than the frame, and a window slides across it while the figure walks in plate space. Travel equal to pan is walking in place. This run travels 326px, which is where the ledge ends — not where the tool gives out.

Two defects found and fixed, both measured
defectbeforeafter
mask offset — hole placement (target 738–1105)633–1010733–1110
pan step, px/frame (ideal 4.592)3.95–5.014.42–4.74
pan step σ0.5060.074

The first defect is the instructive one. The strip adds 100px above the shot, so masks cut against shot-real.png landed 100px high: the clean plate erased empty silk, the real Ge Hong stayed painted in, and a shifted ghost was pasted over him. It looked fine in a contact sheet. Both tools now refuse a mask whose declared size does not match the image unless --mask-offset says where it belongs.

The second was a strobe. Rounding the window to whole pixels made the pan step unevenly; on ink texture that is what makes a pan look machine-made. The window is now sampled at subpixel precision.

Standing

Where this leaves the animation

The deterministic cel stack keeps everything it had and gains a camera. Water, foliage, the standing figure and the walk all run on CPU in seconds and loop. The pan removes the frame as a limit. Nothing in today's work displaces any of it.

What a model may now be trusted with is narrow and real: relief on figures, where it reads form rather than ink. What it still cannot supply is landscape space, and the plane stack cannot either — not because the planes are wrong, but because planes are flat by construction and no amount of blur changes that.

Next

The deer's legs, cut by hand as separate parts with their own pivots and phases, which is what the walk is blocked on. Then two figures under one panning camera, which the current one-figure-per-call shape cannot do — the clean answer is the multiplane camera, elements as RGBA sequences and a camera tool panning the window over plate plus elements.
